headline: Pritzker and Duckworth urge Congress to let hemp THC ban start
dek: An Illinois agenda for the new Congress says the federal hemp THC ban due 11 December should face no more delay, as synthetic cannabinoids lose legal cover on 12 November.
key_points: Gov. JB Pritzker, Senator-elect Juliana Stratton and Sen. Tammy Duckworth published a congressional agenda telling lawmakers to let the federal ban on intoxicating hemp take effect.
The agenda says Congress should oppose any further delay or amendment and should not regulate or legalize intoxicating hemp.
Most hemp THC products lose federal legality on 11 December; synthetic cannabinoids that the plant cannot produce naturally lose it on 12 November.
Missouri's own total THC law, which treats products above 0.3% total THC as marijuana, also starts on 12 November after surviving court challenges.
body: The fight over intoxicating hemp now has a new and influential voice on the side of the ban. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who was elected to the US Senate on 3 November, and Sen. Tammy Duckworth published a policy agenda for the incoming Congress this week that tells lawmakers to let the federal recriminalization of hemp THC products take effect as scheduled.

The document, titled "Fighting for Illinois: Day One Agenda", contains about 200 proposals, according to Marijuana Moment. On hemp, it says Congress should oppose any further delay and any further amendment, and should not further regulate or legalize intoxicating hemp. It argues that children can buy untested products in gas stations and smoke shops and that continued sales undercut Illinois's licensed cannabis businesses, including its social equity licensees.

Congress redefined hemp late last year so that, once the change takes effect, only products with no more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container stay legal. That was originally due on 12 November. A funding law President Trump signed in September moved the date for most products to 11 December, giving lawmakers more time to write rules for hemp derivatives.

One part still lands on 12 November: the exclusion of products containing cannabinoids that are not capable of being naturally produced by the cannabis plant, according to Marijuana Moment. In practice, that targets synthetic cannabinoids on Thursday, 12 November, while plant-derived THC products have until 11 December.

The Illinois agenda arrives as Congress changes hands: the midterms gave Democrats majorities in both chambers, Marijuana Moment reported. The agenda is a marker for that new majority, at a time when hemp businesses are pressing for regulation instead of a ban.
> Illinois wants the ban for the same reason hemp sellers fear it: it protects the licensed cannabis market.
## A split inside one state's delegation

The Illinois position is not as unified as the joint document suggests. In August, Duckworth voted to table an amendment from Sen. Ted Budd, a North Carolina Republican, that sought to strip the delay from a funding bill, which in effect supported postponing the ban, Marijuana Moment reported. Sen. Dick Durbin, whose seat Stratton will take, voted against tabling it.

Others are pushing in the same direction as Pritzker. Former DEA Administrator Asa Hutchinson has written an op-ed urging Congress not to delay recriminalization again, Marijuana Moment noted, and Politico has reported that lobbyists for major alcohol companies urged state attorneys general to press Congress to keep the ban on schedule.
## Illinois has already acted at home

Pritzker signed a broad cannabis law in June that recriminalizes hemp THC products above 0.4 milligrams per container under state law, mirroring the federal limit. That law also doubled adult possession limits, allowed drive-through and curbside pickup at dispensaries, and let medical cannabis certifications be issued by telehealth. We reported on 6 November on the Illinois deadline for hemp sellers.

Illinois is not alone. In Missouri, House Bill 2641 takes effect on 12 November. It classifies any product above 0.3% total THC, including delta-8, delta-9, THCA flower, gummies and vapes, as marijuana that only state-licensed facilities can sell, KQ2 reported. Naturally derived cannabinoid beverages get until 11 December, to match federal law.

Attorney General Catherine Hanaway said on 5 November that the state had successfully defended the law against legal challenges and that people who violate it could face prosecution. The law also bars dispensaries from keeping customers' identifying information without written consent, with a $500 fine per violation, and allows cannabis workers to organize and bargain collectively. As we reported on 6 November, the attorney general has already sued four shops over hemp sales.

For licensed cannabis operators in both states, the effect is the same: products that competed with dispensaries from gas station shelves are being pushed back inside the licensed system, at least on paper. Enforcement, as Missouri's lawsuits show, is what will decide how fast that happens.

On 12 November, synthetic cannabinoid products lose federal cover and Missouri's total THC rule starts. Between then and 11 December, watch for any bill in Congress to delay the federal ban again or replace it with a regulatory framework, and for how the new Democratic leadership handles the issue. The Illinois agenda signals that a delay will not be a simple party-line vote.
